You end with: a single-key wallet made from key 3dca6805, its backup planned on the backup board and carried out with its checklist: the words and the SeedQR copied by hand and checked, a vault made, and the sticks written. USB sticks are not very reliable for long-term storage: name-brand sticks are generally better, and cheap off-brand sticks should not be relied on to keep a backup for years. Always keep a paper or metal backup as well. Seal and label each envelope as the checklist's One envelope per place says. Keep the record of what is at each place. Never write the words on it. t: Before you rely on a key
p: Before you rely on a key
x: Faraday is an offline key store and signer: it keeps a key for one session, and signs what it is shown. What makes a key safe to rely on is its backup, the copy of Faraday that made it, and what is signed with it. This page checks the first two and says what Faraday cannot check. You end with: a key restored once from its backup alone, the Faraday download checked, and a list of what Faraday does not protect against. Before you start: Make a key and Back it up, or, for several keys, Make a wallet as well. You'll need: The Faraday stick, and the PC it starts. The backup of one place: the paper copy of the words, or the vault's stick and its passphrase. The fingerprint written down when the key was made. Time: about 30 minutes.

t: Restore the key once from the backup alone
p: Before you rely on a key
x: A backup is known to work only once a key has come back from it, with nothing else at hand. Power off Faraday. Everything in memory is wiped. Put away everything that is not the backup being checked: no other paper, no note of the words, no second stick. Start the PC from the Faraday stick again. Faraday starts with no key loaded. Load the key from the backup alone: - From paper: press Wallets → Add a key, Change on Start, then Type the words. Type the words from the paper and press Continue. - From a vault: plug the vault's stick in. On Stick visit, press Import 1 file, then pull the stick (Files, sticks and QR codes, step 2). Correct the paper from another place's backup, and restore again another fingerprint the backup gives another key: a wrong word that still makes a valid list, a wrong passphrase, or another key's paper do not rely on the key until a restore gives its fingerprint Repeat this for each place that holds enough to restore the key, and again after a backup is changed.

p: Before you rely on a key
x: A key is only as sound as the Faraday that made it. Check the Starter file before writing a stick from it, as the README's Verifying a release says: import the release key, compare its fingerprint with one from a second place (the README on GitHub and the website, for example), then check the signature of SHA256SUMS and the file's sum. The Starter's About lists the same commands under Checking this file, and the SHA-256 of each image it carries. A file that does not pass the check is not used: download it again.

t: What Faraday does not protect against
p: Before you rely on a key
x: A Faraday program that is not the real one. Checking the download (step 2) is the defence; reproducible builds let others check that the published files come from the published code. A compromised computer below Faraday. Changed firmware, hardware implants, and someone reading the computer's memory just after it is turned off. The management processors some computers carry under the operating system (Intel's Management Engine with AMT, AMD's PSP). Learn: What else runs on this computer. Anything that records the screen or the keys: a smart TV, a capture card, a KVM switch, a camera, or a person watching. Learn: Screens and devices that can record. A weak passphrase on a vault or a key. A wrong address in what is signed. Faraday shows every output and the fee; it cannot know whether an address is the one meant. Read them on Faraday's screen before signing, and check a receive address there. Learn: Verifying. A lost or unreadable backup. Faraday keeps nothing after power off: without a backup that works, the key is gone. Learn: Backups. Someone who asks for the words. No support desk, wallet or person needs them. Learn: Mistakes and scams.

t: Multisig with other people and devices
p: Multisig with other people and devices
x: You end with: key 3dca6805 in a 2-of-3 wallet whose other two keys are held by other people on their own devices, the wallet loaded on Faraday with its first address checked, and a spend signed with your key and sent back for theirs. Before you start: Make a key, Make a wallet (the multisig steps) and Spend. You'll need: Faraday with key 3dca6805 loaded from its paper copy (typed, as Make a wallet, step 5.1, does) and no stick attached. Two cosigners, each with a key on a device of their own. In this walkthrough the public test keys 5d388376 (twenty-four times zebra) and cf2e083d (twenty-four times summer) stand for them. A coordinator: Sparrow, or another wallet that makes a multisig from its cosigners' keys, on an online computer. For the stick ways, a USB stick other than the Faraday stick. Time: about 40 minutes. A multisig wallet is made from each key's public part, its xpub, with the fingerprint and path the key was derived at. A cosigner gives that and keeps the words. A coordinator puts the xpubs together and writes the transactions; each signer signs on its own device.

You end with: a vault of your own on a stick, holding key 3dca6805, a login with its TOTP codes and a note; the vault written, locked and unlocked again, and the login exported for KeePass. Before you start: Make a key. Back it up makes a vault inside a backup's checklist (step 4.8); this page makes one on its own, for keys and for everything else. You'll need: Faraday with key 3dca6805 loaded and no stick attached. A USB stick other than the Faraday stick, formatted FAT32. For a passphrase from dice: five dice, or one die rolled five times. For the codes: a site's TOTP setup code (its QR code or its key), and a phone or watch showing the time to the minute. Time: about 30 minutes. A vault is one file, .fvlt, sealed under one to four passphrases. Faraday opens it in memory, seals it again at every lock, and writes it to a stick on the next stick visit. The passphrases on this page are examples only: never use a passphrase printed anywhere, this page included.

Passphrases, the cost and the space are fixed when a vault is made. To change one, create a new vault, unlock both, and save into the new one what the old one holds: load the keys and wallets and Save them, and add the entries and notes again. Write the new vault, then delete the old file from its stick with zeros (Files, sticks and QR codes): until it is deleted, the old file still opens with the old passphrase. With your own key Roll the passphrase with real dice: six words of the long list. Never use a passphrase printed anywhere, or one used for anything else. Write the passphrase down and keep it apart from the stick: a lost passphrase loses what it opens. Name the vault for whoever may see the stick, or leave the name empty. Before you rely on the vault, unlock it from its stick on a fresh start: Before you rely on a key. A KeePass export is as safe as its passphrase: give it a strong one of its own. Why: Vaults, Passphrases, Time and TOTP codes, Where keys are kept. Next: Files, sticks and QR codes.

You end with: a GPG key, Example Signer , made in a vault kept on two sticks at two places; its public key on a computer; a file signed with it and the signature checked there; and the key's revocation and paperkey where they can be used. Before you start: Vaults, passwords and codes (creating and unlocking a vault) and Files, sticks and QR codes (a stick visit). You'll need: Faraday started from the stick, with no stick attached but the Faraday stick. Two USB sticks other than the Faraday stick, formatted FAT32, one for each place the key is kept at. A phone or watch showing the time to the minute: a GPG key carries the time it was made, and a signature the time it was made. A text file to sign, notes.txt in this walkthrough, on a stick. A computer with GnuPG (Gpg4win on Windows), to check the signature. Time: about 40 minutes. The name, email, file names and passphrases on this page are examples only: use your own. A GPG key cannot be made again from seed words, so Faraday makes it inside the backup: the key is planned at two places or more, written to each, and signs nothing until every place is written. In Faraday Demo, Practice makes no GPG key: Make the key does nothing there (Faraday Demo).

Press Tools, then GPG key (Make, restore, sign, revoke, paperkey). With no vault open, the backup flow opens at once. With a vault open, Vault contents opens on GPG keys instead: press Make a key there (Vault contents). An empty vault offers Make a GPG key too. The flow is a column of cards, each closed to one line once it is done: Where it will be kept, Bring in the sticks, Vaults, Make the key, Lock, Write the sticks and Done. On Check a signed message, read the Address and the Message as well as the verdict: a valid signature over other words, or for another address, proves something else. Why: Signing a message, Mistakes and scams. Next: More from a key.

You end with: key 3dca6805's addresses read at any path; a child seed and a password made from it with BIP-85 and kept in a vault; its silent payments address, record and wallet; an address that begins with characters you chose; a Lightning node key; Seed XOR parts put back together into the key; and randomness of your own added to the session. Before you start: Make a key, Vaults, passwords and codes (a vault made and unlocked) and Files, sticks and QR codes (a stick visit). You'll need: Faraday with key 3dca6805 loaded, as Make a wallet loads it: its row reads 3dca6805 · New key 1. A key typed back in is named by its fingerprint and reads 3dca6805 alone, as in the pictures. With more keys loaded, each tool asks which first. Vault 1 of Vaults, passwords and codes, unlocked, to keep what is made. For step 8, the paper with key 3dca6805's words, or Faraday Demo's sample. Time: about 40 minutes. Each tool here reads a loaded key and changes nothing about it. What it makes comes back the same from the same key, on any device that follows the same standard. In Faraday Demo's Practice the secrets these tools would make are dimmed: BIP-85's values, the vanity passphrase, the Lightning node's private key and the silent payments scan key. The public values all work (Faraday Demo).

Vanity address found for key 3dca6805: bc1q faaq 7qxh … x2nz lm, Account 1017 of this key after 1,018 tries, Open this wallet and Search again Press Vanity address. t: Seed XOR parts back into a key
c: Seed XOR needs two parts or more
x: Add a key · Seed XOR parts with Part 1 and Part 2 in, 12 words each Seed XOR splits a key's words into two or three sets of words, the parts. Every part is needed to make the key again. Each part is itself a valid set of BIP-39 words, a wallet of its own: keep it with the same care as the key's words. To make them, open the key's backup and its copy by hand (Back it up): under Other paper forms, press Seed XOR, 2 parts or Seed XOR, 3 parts. The parts show, "2 parts · every one is needed", each part's words numbered; copy each onto its own paper, then press Put them away. They are new randomness each time, and dimmed in Practice. To put them back into the key, press Tools, then Seed XOR. Add a key opens with Type Seed XOR parts chosen and its typing card open (the other forms): Type the first part's words and press Add this one: "Part 1 · 12 words", under a count of the parts in ("2 in" once there are two). Scan a QR code reads a part instead. Do the same for every other part. Under Passphrase, type the key's BIP-39 passphrase, if it has one. Press Make the key. One part alone reads Seed XOR needs two parts or more. The key loads with its own fingerprint: 3dca6805 for parts made from it. In Practice, Load samples offers "Seed XOR, 2 parts", and Faraday Demo's strip's Use a sample puts a part in as if typed. SLIP-39 shares come back the same way, from Restore from SLIP-39; codex32 strings are codex32 shares.

c: Enough for 256 bits on its own
x: Add randomness on Dice: the six faces, In this batch: 10 dice rolls, Undo, Clear and Add What Faraday makes from randomness (a new key from this device, Seed XOR parts, codex32 shares) takes the system's randomness. Randomness of your own can be mixed in, never in its place. Press Settings. Randomness reads "System: … · your own: none". Press Add randomness. Choose a source: Camera (with a camera attached), Dice, Coins, Cards or Pointer and keys. Enter some: for Dice, type each roll ("Type 1 to 6 · Backspace takes one back · Enter adds"). "In this batch: 10 dice rolls" counts them; at 99 rolls it reads Enough for 256 bits on its own. Undo takes the last back, Clear the batch. Press Add. The line at the top reads "… · your own: 10 dice rolls", and a check mark under the pad reads "Added to the pool once: 10 dice rolls"; each batch after that counts up there. Pointer and keys takes the pointer's moves over its box and the keys typed while it is chosen. What is added is kept for this session only: Lock wipes it. New key's Generator card offers the same sources (Make a key). With your own key A child seed, password or key from BIP-85 is as secret as the key it comes from: whoever has the key's words can make every one of them again. Back up the key as the backup of all of them. Write down each child's application, length and index with what it is for. A child seed used as a wallet on another device needs a backup of its own there, or that note kept with the key's backup. Keep a scan key, a node's private key or a child in a vault. Use Out unprotected… only for the device that needs it, on a stick kept for that. Open an eye in Explore only with no one watching and no camera seeing the screen. Write down the account a vanity search found, and the characters it added to a passphrase: without them the address is not found again. Keep Seed XOR parts at different places: every part is needed, and one lost loses the key. Why: Words, Xpubs and privacy, Silent payments, Passphrases, Backups in other forms, Tools, Randomness. Next: Check and decode.

You end with: the transaction of Spend taken apart field by field, its signatures' nonces checked, an address checked against the loaded wallets, a file's SHA-256 compared with another computer's, and each of the six calculators used once. Before you start: Spend (a transaction signed and finished), Receive (checking an address) and Files, sticks and QR codes (a stick visit). You'll need: Faraday with keys 3dca6805 and 5d388376 loaded and New wallet 1, the 2-of-3 of Make a wallet, loaded. The PSBT of Spend, payment.psbt, signed there to the end, or a finished transaction (.txn) on a stick. A watch-only wallet showing a receive address, as in Receive. For the file check, a computer that prints a file's SHA-256 (sha256sum on Linux and macOS, Get-FileHash on Windows). Time: about 25 minutes. None of these checks signs anything or changes a file. The calculators keep nothing of what is typed in them.

x: Tools with Find a tool at the top and the Keys and seeds and Wallets groups of tiles Press Tools in the sidebar. Tools lists every flow by what it works on, each tile with its name, one line and the standards it follows. What is typed goes into Find a tool: a name, a BIP number at the top: "85" finds BIP-85, and No tool matches shows when nothing does. This walkthrough uses two groups: Group Tiles Transactions Sign a transaction, Nonce check, Decode a transaction, Check an address Calculators Hashes, Encodings, Descriptor checksum, Convert an xpub, Units, Miniscript compiler A tile that needs something first is grey, and its line says what, in the warning tone: Load a wallet first.

x: Decode a transaction finished from payment.psbt: Transaction id, Witness id, Version, Locktime, Size, Fee and Amounts in, one input and two outputs The 2-of-3's payment.psbt, signed with a second key and finished, opened with Decode it: "Finished from payment.psbt", Fee "1850 sat · 9.8 sat/vB", "Inputs · 1", and "Outputs · 2", the payment (Pays out of the loaded wallets) and the change ("Change · back to new-wallet-1-descriptor · 1/0"). The way back reads Back to Spend. Decode a transaction takes apart a transaction that is signed and finished, the one a wallet broadcasts. Open it one of three ways: From Press Spend's Send it card, under the nonce check Decode it Files, a Finished transaction such as payment-final.txn Nonce check, then Decode it Tools Decode a transaction: the first finished transaction in Files, or the camera when there is none; a transaction scanned lands as scanned-1.txn Under the title, where it came from: the file's name, or "Finished from payment.psbt". Then: Row What it is Transaction id the txid, the one a wallet or an explorer reports once it is broadcast Witness id the id with the signatures counted Version the transaction's version Locktime 0 · none, or a block height or a time Size bytes, virtual bytes and weight units Fee in sat and sat/vB; Not stated: the amounts going in are not here when no PSBT of it is Amounts in the PSBT the amounts going in were read from ("From payment.psbt"); Not here; or PSBTs of it state different amounts, and none is used Inputs lists each input from 0: the output it spends, its amount where known, its sequence and what it means (final, locktime on, no replace-by-fee, …), and its witness. Outputs lists each output: its amount, its address, its kind (P2WPKH, P2WSH, P2TR, …), and whose it is: Line Tone Meaning "Change · back to New wallet 1 · 1/0" ok change, to a loaded wallet's change address "Back to New wallet 1 · receive 0/…" ok to a loaded wallet's receive address Pays out of the loaded wallets warning to an address no loaded wallet makes in its first 100 Compare the outputs that pay out with the payee's address and amount. Show the hex shows the whole transaction as hex (Hide the hex hides it); Show as QR shows it as a code, for a wallet or an explorer that broadcasts it.

c: Valid · not the nonce this key makes: do not broadcast
Nonce check · a signature is wrong
Show the finished transaction as QR
Valid · signed elsewhere, its nonce needs that device's key
Valid · no key origin: its nonce is not recomputed
Valid · finalized: its nonce is not recomputed
Invalid: not this key's over this transaction
x: Send it on Spend from New wallet 1, the nonce check reading 2 signatures valid, 2 recomputed here, under the two files The nonce check is on Spend's Send it card, under the files, once the transaction is finished. Tools → Nonce check opens that card. It also checks a transaction another signer made, with nothing signed here. A PSBT that carries signatures and that no key loaded here is left to sign, or a finished transaction, opens on the Nonce check page instead of signing, from every way in: From Press The camera scan it: the page opens, and its way back is to where the scan started Files the row's Nonce check Tools Nonce check, with no spend finished here: the first such file in Files, or the camera The page shows the file's name and the same check as Send it. Under it, unless a signature is wrong: Save to a stick (the finished transaction as payment-final.txn, or the PSBT as it came, For the stick; Remove while it waits there), and for a finished one Decode it, Show the raw hex and Show as QR; a PSBT still wanting signatures reads "Not finished: more signatures are wanted" and offers its code. A wrong signature reads "Not finished: a signature is wrong" and offers nothing to carry on. To use Faraday as a check on another signer, a SeedSigner or a hardware wallet: Open what it signed under Tools → Nonce check (scan its PSBT, or bring the file in on a stick). Every signature is checked against what is in the transaction, and two that share a nonce are refused. For the strong check, load that signer's seed here once (Add a key) and open it again: each of its signatures is signed again here under both nonce rules, and the row says which made it ("Valid · nonce recomputed, low R"). One that neither rule makes reads Valid · not the nonce this key makes: do not broadcast. Its first line sums it up: First line Tone "Nonce check · 2 signatures valid · 2 recomputed here" ok "Nonce check · 1 of 2 signatures not checked" warning Nonce check · a signature is wrong danger Then a row per signature, Input 0, Input 1 and on, with the key and what was found; an input signed by two keys has two rows, as input 0 of the 2-of-3 has in the picture. Under them, Decode it, Show the raw hex and Show the finished transaction as QR. Row Meaning "Valid · nonce recomputed, low R" signed with a key here, and the same signature made again here Valid · signed elsewhere, its nonce needs that device's key valid; its nonce can be checked only on the device that holds the key Valid · no key origin: its nonce is not recomputed valid; the transaction names no origin for its key (a final raw transaction carries none), so no key here is matched to it Valid · finalized: its nonce is not recomputed valid, under a key here, but read from a final witness, which is not signed again Valid · not the nonce this key makes: do not broadcast valid, but not made the way this key signs Invalid: not this key's over this transaction the signature does not hold "Not checked ·" and why it could not be checked here Two signatures that share a nonce are named in red, with the inputs ("one nonce on inputs … · this gives the key away"). Past twelve rows, one line counts the rest ("4 more · none wrong"). A raw transaction is checked against the PSBT of it in Files, which states what its inputs spend; with none, its first line reads "Nonce check · 1 not checked: the outputs they spend are not here".

keys need origins and both chains to load
Pays out of the loaded wallets
x: Tools → Miniscript compiler (A policy compiled into a descriptor) opens Miniscript compiler (the calculators). The field takes a policy: A policy, e.g. or(pk(9a6a2580),and(pk(…),older(1000))). The mode row chooses the script: wsh (SegWit) or tr (Taproot). A loaded key can be named by its fingerprint; with 3dca6805 and 5d388376 loaded, type: or(pk(3dca6805),and(pk(5d388376),older(1000))) 3dca6805 spends at any time; 5d388376 spends once the coins are 1000 blocks old. The page shows: Row What it is Descriptor the policy compiled, with each fingerprint as the loaded key's xpub with its origin, and the checksum Spend paths how many ways it can be spent Wallet one this device loads; or keys need origins and both chains to load, when a key is typed some other way A policy the compiler cannot compile shows its message in red. To use the descriptor as a wallet, load it through Restore an existing wallet (Miniscript and inheritance on Tools leads there). With your own key Read every output of a transaction on Faraday's screen before it is broadcast; an output that Pays out of the loaded wallets is the payment and nothing else. Give out a transaction whose Nonce check reads anything but valid only after finding out why; "do not broadcast" means so. Take receive addresses from Faraday or the watch-only wallet, and check them with Check an address, never from a page or a message. Compare a file's SHA-256 with the one another computer prints for it before you load or sign what is in it. Why: Verifying, Nonces, Tools, Inheritance. Next: The Starter's other tools.

You end with: a file sent from this computer to Faraday by QR code and one received back; a blank template printed and saved as a PDF; a Faraday stick brought to the Starter's release with its data kept; and where the rest of the Starter is. You'll need: Faraday Starter, open on a computer running Windows or Linux, with a camera for step 3. Faraday started from the stick on another computer, with a camera, beside this one. A printer, or a PDF viewer, for step 4. For step 5, a Faraday stick of an earlier release. Time: about 30 minutes. The Starter runs on a computer that is online. With a stick in, Add this key and Add this share are dimmed: "Remove the stick first". A seed read at Restore's Scan it or Create's Scan its xpub goes, after SeedQR read, into the slot of the flow on screen; so does a codex32 secret, loaded with no sheet, since it holds no passphrase; a codex32 string or a SLIP-39 share read by a wallet's Scan a key opens its form for that wallet.
